questions.q: What amplitude pattern must a 2-qubit state [w,x,y,z] fit in order to be a product state?
options: It must be expressible as [ac, ad, bc, bd] for some numbers a, b, c, d, matching w=ac, x=ad, y=bc, z=bd
All four amplitudes must be equal to each other
At least one of the four amplitudes must be exactly zero
The amplitudes must sum to exactly 1 rather than their squares summing to 1
questions.explain: A product state is by definition a tensor product (a|0>+b|1>)⊗(c|0>+d|1>), which expands to [ac, ad, bc, bd] -- so a state is a product state exactly when its amplitudes fit this factored pattern.

questions.q: In the Bell state's amplitude pattern [1/√2, 0, 0, 1/√2] matched against [ac, ad, bc, bd], why does ad = 0 lead to a contradiction no matter which branch (a=0 or d=0) is chosen?
options: If a=0 then ac=0 contradicts the required ac=1/√2; if d=0 then bd=0 contradicts the required bd=1/√2 -- both branches of 'ad=0 means a=0 or d=0' individually clash with a different nonzero requirement
ad=0 has no bearing on the other three equations at all
The contradiction only occurs because 1/√2 is an irrational number
a=0 and d=0 can both be avoided by choosing complex values for b and c instead
questions.explain: Since ad=0 forces a=0 or d=0, and the problem separately requires ac and bd to both be nonzero (1/√2 each), whichever branch is taken zeroes out one of those required nonzero terms -- an unavoidable contradiction.

questions.q: What does it mean, mathematically, for a 2-qubit state to be 'entangled'?
options: It cannot be written as a tensor product of any two single-qubit states -- there is no choice of a, b, c, d that reproduces its amplitudes as [ac, ad, bc, bd]
The two qubits are physically touching each other
It means the state has more than 2 nonzero amplitudes
It means the state cannot be normalized to have probabilities summing to 1
questions.explain: Entanglement is defined purely algebraically: a state is entangled exactly when no factorization into a tensor product of two single-qubit states exists, as proven for the Bell state via the ac/ad/bc/bd contradiction.

questions.q: What amplitude pattern made the Bell state resistant to factoring, as identified in the lesson?
options: Nonzero amplitudes on the 'matching' basis states (|00⟩ and |11⟩) combined with exactly zero amplitude on the 'mismatched' basis states (|01⟩ and |10⟩)
All four amplitudes being exactly equal to each other
Having a negative amplitude on one of the basis states
Having amplitude only on a single basis state
questions.explain: Forcing both cross-terms (ad and bc) to zero while keeping both diagonal terms (ac and bd) nonzero is exactly the condition that makes the ad=0 branch analysis fail for every choice of a,b,c,d -- which is the Bell state's signature pattern.

questions.q: Why is it a mistake to describe entanglement as meaning the two qubits are exchanging a signal or are physically connected?
options: The entanglement proof is a pure statement about whether one vector factors into a tensor product of two smaller vectors -- it never involves distance, time, or signaling; those are physical consequences, not the mathematical definition
Entangled qubits can only exist if physically touching, so the description is actually correct
Entanglement is purely a measurement artifact with no real mathematical basis
Signaling between qubits is required to create entanglement in the first place, making the description accurate
questions.explain: The algebraic non-factorization proof makes no reference to physical distance or communication -- entanglement is a property of the state vector itself, and popular descriptions of 'spooky' correlation describe a downstream physical consequence, not the definition.
